entries.name: Jenisha S. Likansis v. Walmart Inc., et al.

authorities_cited.proposition: Advancement under Section 145 is purely permissive, so the Court considered only contractual mandatory advancement rights under the Bylaws (citing Gilbert v. Unisys Corp., 2024 WL 3789952 (Del. Ch. Aug. 13, 2024), and Holley v. Nipro Diagnostics, Inc., 2014 WL 7336411 (Del. Ch. Dec. 23, 2014)).

Corporate officers have the titles and duties stated in the bylaws or a board resolution. Cited in support of the point that Walmart Connect, as a division, has no officers in the sense the entity statutes contemplate.
An LLC manager holds offices and responsibilities as provided in the LLC agreement. Cited alongside § 142(a) for the same point that officer status derives from the governing instrument.

authorities_cited.authority: Senior Tour Players 207 Mgmt. Co. LLC v. Golftown 207 Hldg. Co., LLC, 853 A.2d 124 (Del. Ch. 2004) (quoting Weinstock v. Lazard Debt Recovery GP, LLC, 2003 WL 21843254 (Del. Ch. Aug. 8, 2003))
authorities_cited.proposition: Summary judgment is an appropriate way to resolve advancement disputes because they turn on the terms of the corporate instruments and the underlying pleadings.

authorities_cited.authority: Bernstein v. TractManager, Inc., 953 A.2d 1003 (Del. Ch. 2007) (quoting Levy v. HLI Operating Co., 924 A.2d 210 (Del. Ch. 2007))
authorities_cited.proposition: Cross-motions do not change the summary judgment standard. Each motion is examined separately, and the movant must show no genuine issue of material fact and entitlement to judgment as a matter of law.

authorities_cited.authority: Tafeen v. Homestore, Inc., 2004 WL 556733 (Del. Ch. Mar. 22, 2004)
authorities_cited.proposition: Unambiguous bylaws are construed as written. The advancement provisions' language controls over the functional characteristics of a claimant's role.

authorities_cited.authority: Jung v. El Tinieblo Int'l, Inc., 2022 WL 16557663 (Del. Ch. Oct. 31, 2022) (citing Emerald Partners v. Berlin, 726 A.2d 1215 (Del. 1999))
authorities_cited.proposition: Failure to raise an argument in an opening brief waives it. Waiver is a matter of discretion and fairness, and a new argument in reply that differs substantively and materially from the opening brief may be deemed waived.

authorities_cited.authority: Franklin Balance Sheet Inv. Fund v. Crowley, 2006 WL 3095952 (Del. Ch. Oct. 19, 2006)
authorities_cited.proposition: A party must set forth all grounds, authorities and arguments supporting its motion in its opening brief.

authorities_cited.authority: Gilbert v. Unisys Corp., 2024 WL 3789952 (Del. Ch. Aug. 13, 2024) (citing Sassano v. CIBC World Mkts. Corp., 948 A.2d 453 (Del. Ch. 2008))
authorities_cited.proposition: 'Another enterprise' may lack formal legal existence, employees, payroll, revenue, or the ability to confer officer titles. On that basis the Court assumed arguendo that an internal division could qualify.

authorities_cited.authority: McLaughlin v. Dover Downs, Inc., 2009 WL 1474707 (Del. 2009) (TABLE)
authorities_cited.proposition: Conclusory assertions lacking probative value, such as appointment by unspecified 'leadership,' do not create a genuine issue of material fact.

authorities_cited.authority: Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.08(a)-(b)
authorities_cited.proposition: The LLC Operating Agreement's indemnification clause (§ 3.7) incorporates California law. California mandates indemnification only for members and managers and makes it permissive for officers, employees and agents, so § 3.7 created no fact dispute.
The Court weighed the post-argument declaration and documents for the weight and credibility they deserved and overruled Plaintiff's objection.
The parties consented to voluntary final adjudication before a Magistrate in Chancery, so the report issues as an opinion subject to ordinary appellate review.

summary.brief_summary: A former Walmart Connect 'Chief of Staff' (pro se), named in a New Jersey discrimination suit, sued Walmart Inc. for mandatory advancement under its Bylaws, and the parties cross-moved for summary judgment before a Magistrate in Chancery sitting by consent for final adjudication under 10 Del. C. § 350. The Court held that officer status turns on appointment by the body the governing instrument designates (Walmart's Board or CEO, or the LLC's defined 'Manager'), not on whether the role was 'officer-like,' and that Plaintiff's admitted appointment by a division head defeated all three of her theories, with her delegation argument waived as first raised in reply. For practitioners, advancement claimants must prove a formal appointment chain under the operative bylaws or LLC agreement and must raise delegation or other alternative appointment theories in the opening brief, while companies can defeat 'functional officer' claims with SEC filings and manager consents even when they bear the burden.
summary.core_legal_issue: Whether a former Walmart employee holding a 'Chief of Staff' title at Walmart Connect, an internal division, qualified for mandatory advancement under Walmart's Bylaws (art. VI, § 2(a)) as an 'officer of the Corporation' or as a person serving 'at the request of the Corporation' as an officer of 'another enterprise' (Walmart Connect or Wal-Mart.com USA, LLC). The question was whether officer status turns on appointment by the body the governing instrument designates (Walmart's Board or CEO, or the LLC's defined 'Manager') rather than on the functional, 'officer-like' nature of the role.
summary.holding: Plaintiff's motion for summary judgment was denied and Walmart's cross-motion was granted under the Rule 56 standard (no genuine issue of material fact; judgment as a matter of law), with Defendants bearing the burden on both motions under Bylaws art. VI, § 5(d). The Bylaws are unambiguous: officers must be appointed by Walmart's Board or, within limited categories, its CEO. Plaintiff conceded she was appointed by Lehrfeld, who was neither. As to Walmart Connect, assuming arguendo it is 'another enterprise,' the same Walmart appointment rules apply. As to Walmart LLC, officers must be elected by the defined 'Manager,' and Lehrfeld was not the Manager. Plaintiff's delegation-of-authority theory under art. IV, § 11 was waived because it was raised first in reply. The Court declined to find waiver of the Walmart LLC theory because Plaintiff first obtained the Operating Agreement with Defendants' reply. The Court did not reach the 'at the request of' element. No remedy or fee award was granted.

entries.name: US INFRA SVCS Buyer, LLC, et al. v. JDB Capital Partners, LLC, et al.

authorities_cited.authority: Ct. Ch. R. 56(a)
authorities_cited.proposition: Summary judgment may be appropriate if the movant shows there is no genuine dispute as to any material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.

authorities_cited.authority: Telxon Corp. v. Meyerson, 802 A.2d 257, 262 (Del. 2002)
authorities_cited.proposition: There is no 'right' to a summary judgment.

authorities_cited.authority: In re El Paso Pipeline P'rs, L.P. Deriv. Litig., 2014 WL 2768782, at *9 (Del. Ch. June 12, 2014)
authorities_cited.proposition: The court may, in its discretion, deny summary judgment if, on preliminary examination, it is desirable to inquire into and develop the facts more thoroughly at trial to clarify the law or its application.

authorities_cited.authority: Orloff v. Shulman, 2007 WL 1862742, at *1 (Del. Ch. June 20, 2007)
authorities_cited.proposition: The court denies requests for leave to file summary judgment motions where such proceedings are apt to waste, rather than conserve, the resources of the parties and the court.

authorities_cited.authority: In re Tri-Star Pictures, Inc., Litig., 1995 WL 106520, at *5 (Del. Ch. Mar. 9, 1995)
authorities_cited.proposition: Even apart from factual disputes, summary judgment may be denied where a more thorough exploration of the facts is needed to properly apply the law to the circumstances.

authorities_cited.authority: MKE Hldgs., Ltd. v. Schwartz, 2024 WL 3964332, at *3 (Del. Ch. Aug. 28, 2024)
authorities_cited.proposition: It may be beneficial to inquire into the facts more thoroughly at trial to clarify whether there is a basis for tolling the statute of limitations.

authorities_cited.authority: Doctrine of fraudulent concealment (tolling)
authorities_cited.proposition: Plaintiffs invoked it to toll limitations until their 2022 discovery of the fraud. The Court held its application here is fact-intensive and better resolved on a trial record.

summary.brief_summary: Defendant JDB Capital Partners sought leave to move for summary judgment on laches and limitations defenses against purchaser plaintiffs US INFRA SVCS Buyer, LLC and US INFRA SVCS, Inc. and intervenor AIG Specialty Insurance Company, who opposed the request; the motion-to-dismiss stage was resolved in January 2025 and trial is set for December 2026. Vice Chancellor Will found that JDB's alleged pre-closing participation in the 'phantom revenue' scheme turns on intent and witness credibility that cannot be decided on a paper record, and that fraudulent-concealment tolling is fact-intensive enough to warrant a full trial record, so JDB lacked good cause to brief summary judgment. Practitioners should expect the Court of Chancery, in its discretion, to refuse leave for pre-trial summary judgment on limitations and tolling defenses where scienter or concealment is disputed and trial is imminent, and should plan to try those defenses rather than rely on dispositive motion practice.
summary.core_legal_issue: Whether defendant JDB Capital Partners showed good cause for leave to move for summary judgment on its laches and statute of limitations defenses. JDB argued the claims are time-barred because it engaged in no affirmative post-closing concealment and non-parties' post-closing acts cannot be imputed to it. Plaintiffs countered that fraudulent concealment tolled limitations, relying on JDB's alleged orchestration of a pre-closing 'phantom revenue' scheme.
summary.holding: Request for leave to move for summary judgment denied. Standard: whether the movant showed good cause to proceed with summary judgment briefing, judged against the Rule 56(a) standard and the court's discretion to deny summary judgment where fuller factual development is desirable. The Court found genuine disputes of material fact on JDB's participation in the alleged fraud, including intent and credibility questions about its pre-closing conduct. It also found the tolling analysis fact-intensive, so briefing would likely be inefficient. The case proceeds to the December 2026 trial. The parties must file a joint letter within five business days identifying which pending discovery motions are withdrawn and which must still be resolved. No fee award.

entries.name: Forian Holdings LLC, et al. v. Symphony Health Solutions Corporation, et al.

authorities_cited.authority: Comcast Cable Commc'ns Mgmt., LLC v. CX360, Inc., 2025 WL 79953 (Del. Ch. Jan. 13, 2025)
authorities_cited.proposition: A bond should not be set based on speculative harm from customers that could hypothetically be lost because of a status quo order; cited to reject the $25 million lost-revenue component, and with the court's own reasoning to reject the Supplier A liquidated-damages component.

authorities_cited.authority: Guzzetta v. Serv. Corp. of Westover Hills, 7 A.3d 467, 470 (Del. 2010) (citing Mead Johnson & Co. v. Abbott Lab'ys, 201 F.3d 883, 888 (7th Cir. 2000))
authorities_cited.proposition: Because a bond effectively caps the damages recoverable by a wrongfully enjoined party, the court should 'err on the high side' in setting it.

summary.brief_summary: Following entry of a preliminary injunction in this dispute between Forian and Symphony Health, Vice Chancellor Will resolved competing letter submissions on bond: plaintiffs proposed four months of MSA fees ($874,000) and defendants sought $158.75 million, after the TRO bond had been set at two months of fees ($437,000). The court held that the TRO-stage MSA-fee methodology remains the most accurate economic proxy for the parties' relationship, and rejected defendants' figure because the Supplier A liquidated damages are inapplicable under a court-order carve-out and the customer-loss theory is unsupported speculation; under Guzzetta's 'err on the high side' principle, it extended the period to nine months to cover the case through a post-trial decision, setting the bond at $1,966,500. Defendants seeking an outsized bond must tie claimed exposure to concrete, non-carved-out contractual liability and identified customer harm, and both sides should expect the court to size the bond to the realistic duration of the injunction through post-trial decision, with leave to seek an increase if the case runs longer.
summary.core_legal_issue: Amount of security required to support a preliminary injunction maintaining the status quo through trial and post-trial decision: specifically, whether the bond should be calibrated to the TRO-stage methodology of monthly MSA fees (and over what period), or instead to defendants' claimed exposure of $133.75 million in liquidated damages under a third-party supplier agreement plus $25 million in speculative downstream customer losses.
summary.holding: The court set the preliminary injunction bond at $1,966,500, rejecting both defendants' proposed $158.75 million and plaintiffs' proposed $874,000. Its figure is nine months at the established $218,500 monthly MSA fee baseline. Supplier A liquidated damages were excluded because, as defendants acknowledged, that agreement carves out use-case restrictions imposed under a court order. Downstream customer losses were excluded because no customer has threatened to defect and no affected agreements were identified. Nine months reflects the anticipated time for discovery, trial and a post-trial decision. If the existing $437,000 TRO bond remains posted, plaintiffs need post only the difference. Defendants may move to increase the bond if the injunction remains in effect beyond that period. Standard of review: Not stated beyond the court's discretionary 'err on the high side' principle.
